title: Representing a Moving Scene
blurb: Rigid-body motion, the Lie group SO(3) and its algebra so(3), the exponential map and Rodrigues' formula, twists in SE(3), velocity transformation — plus the alternatives (Euler angles, quaternions) and why gimbal lock matters.

knowledge_points.title: Rigid-Body Motion and What It Preserves
knowledge_points.recap:
**Definition.** A rigid-body motion is a map $g:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ that preserves the **distance** between any two points **and** the **orientation** (handedness) of the frame. Written on vectors, the two defining properties are
$$\|g_*(v)\|=\|v\|\quad\text{(norm / length)},\qquad g_*(v)\times g_*(w)=g_*(v\times w)\quad\text{(cross product / orientation)}.$$
The second condition is what rules out reflections: an orthogonal map preserving lengths but flipping the cross product is a mirror, not a motion.
**Consequence.** Preserving lengths ⇒ preserving inner products (polarisation: $\langle u,v\rangle=\tfrac12(\|u+v\|^2-\|u\|^2-\|v\|^2)$), so the linear part is orthogonal; adding the cross-product condition forces $\det=+1$, i.e. $R\in SO(3)$. Hence every rigid-body motion is $x\mapsto Rx+T$ with $R\in SO(3)$, $T\in\mathbb{R}^3$ — the group $SE(3)$.
**Cross product and the hat operator.** $u\times v=\hat uv$ with $\hat u$ skew-symmetric (Ch. 1). Useful identities: $u\times v=-v\times u$, $u\times u=0$, $\langle u\times v,u\rangle=0$, and the BAC–CAB rule $a\times(b\times c)=b(a^\top c)-c(a^\top b)$.
**Rotation and the cross product.** For $R\in SO(3)$: $R(v\times w)=(Rv)\times(Rw)$ and the conjugation identity $R\hat uR^\top=\widehat{Ru}$ — both appear repeatedly when manipulating the essential matrix.
**Quadratic-form fact.** $x^\top M_1x=x^\top M_2x$ for all $x$ **iff** $M_1-M_2$ is skew-symmetric — the same "quadratic forms only see the symmetric part" statement as in Chapter 1.

questions.q: Write down two equations with respect to any two vectors $v,w\in\mathbb{R}^3$ to show the properties that a rigid-body motion needs to preserve.
questions.answer:
**Preservation of norm / length:**
$$\|g(v)\|=\|v\|.$$
**Preservation of the cross product / orientation:**
$$g(v\times w)=g(v)\times g(w).$$
**Why both.** The first alone only gives $R\in O(3)$ — reflections included. The cross-product condition forces $\det(R)=+1$, restricting to $SO(3)$, i.e. proper rigid motions.
questions.extend: Length alone ⇒ orthogonal; length **and** cross product ⇒ rotation. That is exactly the difference between $E(3)$ and $SE(3)$.

questions.q: Given a rotation matrix $R\in SO(3)$, show that it preserves distances: $\|Rv\|=\|v\|$ for all $v\in\mathbb{R}^3$.
questions.answer:
$$\|Rv\|^2=(Rv)^\top(Rv)=v^\top R^\top Rv=v^\top Iv=\|v\|^2,$$
using $R^\top R=I$. Taking square roots (both sides non-negative) gives $\|Rv\|=\|v\|$.
questions.extend: The same computation with two different vectors gives $\langle Rv,Rw\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle$ — rotations preserve angles as well as lengths.

questions.q: Let $M_1,M_2\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$. Prove that $x^\top M_1x=x^\top M_2x$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^3$ if and only if $M_1-M_2$ is skew-symmetric.
questions.answer:
Write $S=M_1-M_2$; the claim is $x^\top Sx=0\ \forall x\iff S^\top=-S$.
**($\Leftarrow$)** If $S$ is skew-symmetric then $x^\top Sx=(x^\top Sx)^\top=x^\top S^\top x=-x^\top Sx$, so $x^\top Sx=0$.
**($\Rightarrow$)** Suppose $x^\top Sx=0$ for all $x$. Taking $x=e_i$ gives $s_{ii}=0$. Taking $x=e_i+e_j$ gives $0=s_{ii}+s_{ij}+s_{ji}+s_{jj}=s_{ij}+s_{ji}$, i.e. $s_{ij}=-s_{ji}$. Hence $S$ is skew-symmetric.
questions.extend: The forward direction needs *two* clever choices of $x$: the basis vectors kill the diagonal, their sums pair up the off-diagonals.

questions.q: Which of the following identities hold for all $R\in SO(3)$ and $u,v,w\in\mathbb{R}^3$?
questions.answer:
**True.** $R(v\times w)=(Rv)\times(Rw)$ — rotations preserve the cross product (this is exactly the orientation condition). $R\hat uR^\top=\widehat{Ru}$ — the conjugation identity, used constantly when rewriting $\hat TR$. $\langle u\times v,u\rangle=0$ — the cross product is orthogonal to its factors.
**False.** $\hat u\hat v=\hat v\hat u$ is wrong: skew-symmetric matrices do not commute in general (their commutator is again a cross product, $[\hat u,\hat v]=\widehat{u\times v}$, which is the Lie bracket of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$).

knowledge_points.title: SO(3): Recognising and Handling Rotation Matrices
knowledge_points.recap:
**Definition.** $SO(3)=\{R\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}\mid R^\top R=I,\ \det(R)=+1\}$.
**Checklist for "is this a rotation matrix?"** (1) square, (2) columns (equivalently rows) **orthonormal** — unit length and mutually orthogonal, (3) $\det=+1$. A matrix that passes (1)–(2) but has $\det=-1$ is a **reflection**, in $O(3)\setminus SO(3)$: e.g. $-I_{3\times3}$ has $\det=-1$ in odd dimensions.
**Handy examples.** $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.6\\-0.6&0.8\end{pmatrix}$ are 2D rotations ($\cos^2+\sin^2=1$, $\det=1$); $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is orthogonal but has $\det=-1$; $\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.5\\-0.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}$ has columns of length $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\neq1$.
**$SO(3)$ is a group but not a vector space.** It is **not** closed under addition or averaging: $\tfrac12(R_1+R_2)$ is generally **not** a rotation (it violates $R^\top R=I$ and $\det=1$ — e.g. $R_1=I$, $R_2=-\!$ a $180^\circ$ rotation gives a singular average). Correct averaging goes through the SVD projection $R^\star=U\operatorname{diag}(1,1,\det(UV^\top))V^\top$ from Chapter 1, or through quaternions.
**Extracting angle and axis.** For $R\in SO(3)$ representing a rotation by $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ about the unit axis $\vec u$:
$$\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{trace}(R)-1}{2}\right),\qquad \vec u=\frac{1}{2\sin\theta}\,(r_{32}-r_{23},\ r_{13}-r_{31},\ r_{21}-r_{12})^\top.$$
Watch three details: it is $\cos^{-1}$ (not $\cos$), the divisor is $2\sin\theta$ (not $\sin\theta$), and the component order is $(32{-}23,\,13{-}31,\,21{-}12)$ — this is exactly the vector whose hat matrix is the skew part $\tfrac12(R-R^\top)$.
**Degrees of freedom.** $R$ has $9$ entries with $6$ constraints ($R^\top R=I$ gives $6$ independent equations), leaving $3$ DOF — matching $\dim\mathfrak{so}(3)=3$.

questions.q: Which of the following matrices are rotation matrices?
questions.answer:
The rotation matrices are $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.6\\-0.6&0.8\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{0.5}&-\sqrt{0.5}&0\\\sqrt{0.5}&\sqrt{0.5}&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
**Why the others fail.** $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is orthogonal but $\det=-1$ (a reflection). $\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.5\\-0.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}$ has columns of norm $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\neq1$, so $R^\top R\neq I$. $-I_{3\times3}$ has $\det=(-1)^3=-1$, again a reflection (a point reflection in odd dimension).
**Procedure.** Check orthonormal columns first (cheap), then the determinant sign.
questions.extend: In **even** dimension $-I$ *is* a rotation ($\det=+1$); in odd dimension it is not. The exam likes that asymmetry.

questions.q: Given any two rotation matrices $R_1,R_2\in SO(3)$, is the average matrix $R=\tfrac12(R_1+R_2)$ always a valid rotation matrix? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
**No.**
**Requirements.** A valid rotation matrix must be orthogonal, $R^\top R=I$, and have determinant $+1$.
**Failure.** The average of two rotation matrices is still a square matrix, but it need not satisfy either condition — $SO(3)$ is a curved manifold, not a linear subspace, so it is not closed under addition or convex combination.
**Counterexample.** Take $R_1=I$ and $R_2=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ (a $180^\circ$ rotation about $z$). Then $R=\tfrac12(R_1+R_2)=\operatorname{diag}(0,0,1)$, which is singular — $\det(R)=0\neq1$.
**How to do it properly.** Project the average back with the SVD: $R^\star=U\operatorname{diag}(1,1,\det(UV^\top))V^\top$, or average unit quaternions and renormalise.
questions.extend: Saying only "$SO(3)$ is not closed under summation" earns partial credit — the marking scheme wants the definition **and** a concrete counterexample.

questions.q: Let $R=(r_{ij})\in SO(3)$ represent a rotation by an angle $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ around an axis spanned by a unit vector $\vec u$. Which of the following gives the correct expressions for $\theta$ and $\vec u$?
questions.answer:
$$\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{trace}(R)-1}{2}\right),\qquad \vec u=\frac{1}{2\sin\theta}\big(r_{32}-r_{23},\ r_{13}-r_{31},\ r_{21}-r_{12}\big)^\top.$$
**Where it comes from.** Rodrigues gives $\operatorname{trace}(R)=1+2\cos\theta$, hence the angle formula; and the skew part $\tfrac12(R-R^\top)=\sin\theta\,\hat u$, whose hat-vector read-off produces the axis with the factor $\tfrac1{2\sin\theta}$.
**Three traps.** It is $\cos^{-1}$, not $\cos$; the denominator is $2\sin\theta$, not $\sin\theta$; and the component order is $(r_{32}-r_{23},\,r_{13}-r_{31},\,r_{21}-r_{12})$ — swapping the last two entries is the usual decoy.

questions.q: The matrix of a rotation in the plane by angle $\theta$ is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$. Let $R\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ correspond to a rotation around the $z$-axis by $\alpha$, **followed by** a rotation around the $x$-axis by $\gamma$. Write $R$ in terms of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$.
questions.answer:
The later rotation is applied **on the left**, so $R=R_x(\gamma)R_z(\alpha)$ with
$$R_z(\alpha)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha&0\\\sin\alpha&\cos\alpha&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_x(\gamma)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos\gamma&-\sin\gamma\\0&\sin\gamma&\cos\gamma\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Multiplying out:**
$$R=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha&0\\\cos\gamma\sin\alpha&\cos\gamma\cos\alpha&-\sin\gamma\\\sin\gamma\sin\alpha&\sin\gamma\cos\alpha&\cos\gamma\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Order matters.** The reverse order, $R_z(\alpha)R_x(\gamma)$ (rotate about $x$ first), gives a different matrix and only earns partial credit.
questions.extend: Read right to left: the **first** rotation is the rightmost factor. Sanity-check with $\gamma=0$, which must return $R_z(\alpha)$.

knowledge_points.title: Lie Algebra so(3), the Exponential Map and Rodrigues' Formula
knowledge_points.recap:
**Lie group / Lie algebra.** $SO(3)$ is a Lie group — a group that is also a smooth manifold. Its Lie algebra is its **tangent space at the identity**:
$$\mathfrak{so}(3)=\{\hat\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}\mid\hat\omega^\top=-\hat\omega\},\qquad\dim\mathfrak{so}(3)=3.$$
Dimensions worth memorising: $\dim\mathfrak{so}(n)=\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ (so $\dim\mathfrak{so}(2)=1$, $\dim\mathfrak{so}(3)=3$), and $\dim\mathfrak{se}(n)=\dim\mathfrak{so}(n)+n$, so $\dim\mathfrak{se}(3)=6$ (**not** $9$) and $\dim\mathfrak{se}(n)-\dim\mathfrak{so}(n)=n$.
**Where it comes from.** Differentiating $R(t)R(t)^\top=I$ gives $\dot RR^\top=-(\dot RR^\top)^\top$, i.e. $\dot RR^\top$ is skew-symmetric — so $\dot R=\hat\omega R$, and the solution through $R(0)=I$ is the matrix exponential.
**Exponential map.** $\exp:\mathfrak{so}(3)\to SO(3)$, $\hat\omega\mapsto e^{\hat\omega}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\hat\omega^n}{n!}$ — note the sum starts at $n=0$ (the $I$ term); starting at $n=1$ is a standard MC decoy. It is **surjective but not injective**: $e^{\hat\omega_1}=e^{\hat\omega_2}$ does **not** imply $\omega_1=\omega_2$ (add $2\pi$ to the angle). Always true: $\exp(-\hat\omega)=(\exp\hat\omega)^{-1}$. **False in general:** $\exp(\hat\omega_1)\exp(\hat\omega_2)=\exp(\hat\omega_1+\hat\omega_2)$ — that only holds when the two commute (see Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff).
**Powers of $\hat\omega$ for $\|\omega\|=1$.** $\hat\omega^2=\omega\omega^\top-I$, $\hat\omega^3=-\hat\omega$, and generally $\hat\omega^{2k+1}=(-1)^k\hat\omega$ (odd), $\hat\omega^{2k}=(-1)^{k-1}\hat\omega^2$ for $k\ge1$ (even).
**Rodrigues' formula.** Grouping the Taylor series into odd and even powers gives
$$e^{\hat\omega}=I+\frac{\hat\omega}{\|\omega\|}\sin(\|\omega\|)+\frac{\hat\omega^2}{\|\omega\|^2}\big(1-\cos(\|\omega\|)\big).$$
Write $\omega=\theta u$ with $\|u\|=1$: the rotation is by angle $\theta=\|\omega\|$ about axis $u$.
**Logarithm of $SO(3)$.** Given $R\neq I$, $\|\omega\|=\theta=\cos^{-1}\big(\tfrac{\operatorname{trace}(R)-1}{2}\big)$ and $\frac{\omega}{\|\omega\|}=\frac{1}{2\sin\theta}(r_{32}-r_{23},r_{13}-r_{31},r_{21}-r_{12})^\top$. For $R=I$, $\omega=0$. The logarithm is **not unique** — $\theta$ and $\theta+2\pi k$, or $\pm$ the axis at $\theta=\pi$, all work.

questions.q: Consider the Lie groups $SE(n)$ and $SO(n)$ with $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and the corresponding Lie algebras $\mathfrak{se}(n)$ and $\mathfrak{so}(n)$. Which of the following statements are correct?
questions.answer:
Correct: $\dim(\mathfrak{so}(2))=1$, $\dim(\mathfrak{se}(n))-\dim(\mathfrak{so}(n))=n$, $\dim(\mathfrak{so}(n))=\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$.
**Incorrect:** $\dim(\mathfrak{se}(3))=9$ — the correct value is $6$ (three rotational plus three translational degrees of freedom).
**Systematic count.** $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ = skew-symmetric $n\times n$ matrices, dimension $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$; $\mathfrak{se}(n)$ adds an $n$-vector of translation, so $\dim\mathfrak{se}(n)=\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}+n$. Hence $\dim\mathfrak{so}(2)=1$, $\dim\mathfrak{so}(3)=3$, $\dim\mathfrak{se}(3)=6$.
questions.extend: A twist $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^6$ — 3 for rotation, 3 for translation — is the direct statement of $\dim\mathfrak{se}(3)=6$.

questions.q: Let $\xi_1,\xi_2\in\mathbb{R}^6$ represent rigid-body motions, $\widehat{\ \cdot\ }:\mathbb{R}^6\to\mathfrak{se}(3)$ the mapping to the Lie algebra, and $\exp:\mathfrak{se}(3)\to SE(3)\subset\mathbb{R}^{4\times4}$ the exponential map. Which of the following statements hold?
questions.answer:
Only $\exp(-\hat\xi_1)=\big(\exp\hat\xi_1\big)^{-1}$.
**Why the others fail.**
$\exp(\hat\xi_1)=\exp(\hat\xi_2)\iff\xi_1=\xi_2$ is **false** — the exponential map is surjective but **not injective**: adding $2\pi$ to a rotation angle gives the same group element.
$\exp(\hat\xi_1)\exp(\hat\xi_2)=\exp(\hat\xi_1+\hat\xi_2)$ is **false** in general — it only holds when $\hat\xi_1$ and $\hat\xi_2$ commute (rigid motions do not).
$\exp(\hat\xi_1)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\hat\xi_1^n}{n!}$ is **false**: the series starts at $n=0$, contributing the identity term $I$.
questions.extend: Two traps in one question: the summation index (must start at $0$) and the non-commutativity of the exponential.

questions.q: Let $R\in SO(3)$ be a rotation around the $z$-axis with an angle of $\pi$. Give a vector $v\in\mathbb{R}^3$ such that $\hat v=\log(R)$, and write down the skew-symmetric matrix $\hat v$, using $\hat u=\begin{pmatrix}0&-u_3&u_2\\u_3&0&-u_1\\-u_2&u_1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.answer:
The rotation axis is $z$ and the angle is $\pi$, so
$$v=\pm\pi(0,0,1)^\top,\qquad \hat v=\pm\pi\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Why $\pm$.** At $\theta=\pi$ a rotation by $+\pi$ and by $-\pi$ about the same axis coincide, so the logarithm is not unique — both signs are accepted.
**Structure check.** $\|v\|=\pi$ encodes the angle, $v/\|v\|=(0,0,1)^\top$ encodes the axis.
questions.extend: In exponential coordinates the *direction* of $\omega$ is the axis and its *norm* is the angle. That single sentence answers most log/exp questions.

questions.q: Compute the rotation matrix $R$ of the previous question ($\pi$ about the $z$-axis) using Rodrigues' rotation formula $e^{\hat\omega}=I+\frac{\hat\omega}{\|\omega\|}\sin(\|\omega\|)+\frac{\hat\omega^2}{\|\omega\|^2}\big(1-\cos(\|\omega\|)\big)$.
questions.answer:
With $\|\omega\|=\pi$: $\sin(\pi)=0$ kills the middle term, and $1-\cos(\pi)=2$, so
$$R=e^{\hat v}=I+\frac{\hat v}{\pi}\sin(\pi)+\frac{\hat v^2}{\pi^2}\big(1-\cos\pi\big)=I+\frac{2}{\pi^2}\hat v^2.$$
**With** $\hat v^2=\pi^2\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$:
$$R=I+2\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Sanity check.** $R^\top R=I$, $\det(R)=+1$, $\operatorname{trace}(R)=-1=1+2\cos\pi$ ✓, and the $z$-axis is fixed ✓.
questions.extend: For $\theta=\pi$ the $\sin$ term always vanishes and the formula collapses to $R=I+2\hat u^2=2uu^\top-I$ — the reflection-like form of a half-turn.

questions.q: Let $w\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and let $I_{3\times3}$ be the identity. Consider $\ ?\ =I_{3\times3}+\frac{\hat w}{\|w\|}\sin(\|w\|)+\frac{\hat w^2}{\|w\|^2}\big(1-\cos(\|w\|)\big)$. Name the equation and complete the left-hand side so that it holds for arbitrary $w$ (the left-hand side may depend only on $\hat w$, not on $w$).
questions.answer:
The equation is **Rodrigues' formula**, and the left-hand side is
$$e^{\hat w}.$$
**Reading.** It converts exponential coordinates (axis $w/\|w\|$, angle $\|w\|$) into the rotation matrix, i.e. it evaluates $\exp:\mathfrak{so}(3)\to SO(3)$ in closed form instead of summing the infinite series.

questions.q: Consider $\omega\in\mathbb{R}^3$ with $\|\omega\|=1$ and its skew-symmetric matrix $\hat\omega$. (a) Show $\hat\omega^2=\omega\omega^\top-I$ and $\hat\omega^3=-\hat\omega$. (b) Find simple rules for $\hat\omega^n$ for all $n\ge1$, distinguishing odd and even $n$. (c) Using $e^A=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{A^k}{k!}$, derive Rodrigues' formula for arbitrary $\omega$.
questions.answer:
**(a)** Using $\hat\omega v=\omega\times v$ and the BAC–CAB rule,
$$\hat\omega^2v=\omega\times(\omega\times v)=\omega(\omega^\top v)-v(\omega^\top\omega)=(\omega\omega^\top-I)v.$$
Then $\hat\omega^3=\hat\omega(\omega\omega^\top-I)=(\hat\omega\omega)\omega^\top-\hat\omega=0-\hat\omega=-\hat\omega$, since $\hat\omega\omega=\omega\times\omega=0$.
**(b)** Odd powers: $\hat\omega^{2k+1}=(-1)^k\hat\omega$. Even powers: $\hat\omega^{2k}=(-1)^{k-1}\hat\omega^2$ for $k\ge1$.
**(c)** For $\|\omega\|=1$, split the series into odd and even powers:
$$e^{\hat\omega}=I+\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\hat\omega^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}+\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\hat\omega^{2k}}{(2k)!}=I+\hat\omega\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^k}{(2k+1)!}+\hat\omega^2\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{(2k)!}=I+\hat\omega\sin1+\hat\omega^2(1-\cos1).$$
For general $\omega$ write $\omega=\theta u$ with $\|u\|=1$, $\theta=\|\omega\|$:
$$e^{\hat\omega}=e^{\theta\hat u}=I+\hat u\sin\theta+\hat u^2(1-\cos\theta)=I+\frac{\hat\omega}{\|\omega\|}\sin\|\omega\|+\frac{\hat\omega^2}{\|\omega\|^2}\big(1-\cos\|\omega\|\big).$$
questions.extend: The two power rules are exactly what make the odd sum collapse to $\sin$ and the even sum to $1-\cos$ — that is the whole derivation.

questions.q: Why is the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ exactly the set of skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrices? Derive it.
questions.answer:
**Setup.** Take a smooth curve $R(t)\in SO(3)$ with $R(0)=I$. Every point on it satisfies the constraint $R(t)R(t)^\top=I$.
**Differentiate.** $\dot RR^\top+R\dot R^\top=0$, i.e. $\dot RR^\top=-\big(\dot RR^\top\big)^\top$ — so $\dot RR^\top$ is **skew-symmetric**. Call it $\hat\omega$.
**At the identity.** $t=0$ gives $\dot R(0)=\hat\omega$, so the tangent space at $I$ is precisely the skew-symmetric matrices:
$$\mathfrak{so}(3)=\{\hat\omega\mid\hat\omega^\top=-\hat\omega\},\qquad\dim=3.$$
**Consequence.** The ODE $\dot R=\hat\omega R$ with $R(0)=I$ has solution $R(t)=e^{\hat\omega t}$ — the exponential map, evaluated in closed form by Rodrigues' formula. Physically $\hat\omega$ is the (constant) angular velocity in body coordinates.

knowledge_points.title: SE(3), Twists and Exponential Coordinates
knowledge_points.recap:
**Rigid-body motion in homogeneous coordinates.** For $R\in SO(3)$, $T\in\mathbb{R}^3$:
$$g=\begin{pmatrix}R&T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\in SE(3),\qquad g^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}R^\top&-R^\top T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
The inverse uses $R^\top$ (= $R^{-1}$) **and** the compensating $-R^\top T$ — writing $-T$ is the classic error.
**Composition order matters.** "Rotate by $R$, then translate by $T$" is $\begin{pmatrix}R&T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$; "translate by $T$, then rotate by $R$" is $\begin{pmatrix}R&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I&T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}R&RT\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ — note the $RT$.
**Lie algebra of twists.** $\mathfrak{se}(3)=\left\{\hat\xi=\begin{pmatrix}\hat\omega&v\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\ \middle|\ \hat\omega\in\mathfrak{so}(3),\ v\in\mathbb{R}^3\right\}$, a $6$-dimensional space. The **twist coordinates** are $\xi=(v,\omega)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^6$: $\omega$ is the angular part, $v$ the linear part (which is **not** simply the translation $T$).
**Exponential coordinates for $SE(3)$.** $\exp(\hat\xi)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{\hat\omega}&Jv\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ where, for $\omega\neq0$, $J=I+\frac{\hat\omega}{\|\omega\|^2}(1-\cos\|\omega\|)+\frac{\hat\omega^2}{\|\omega\|^3}(\|\omega\|-\sin\|\omega\|)$; for $\omega=0$ it degenerates to pure translation $T=v$. Conversely every $g\in SE(3)$ has (non-unique) exponential coordinates — $\exp:\mathfrak{se}(3)\to SE(3)$ is surjective but not injective.
**Why it matters downstream.** Optimising over $SE(3)$ (bundle adjustment, direct SLAM) is done by *left-multiplying* an incremental $\exp(\hat\xi)$: the $6$ twist coordinates are an unconstrained local parameterisation, which is exactly what a Gauss–Newton step needs.

questions.q: Given a rotation matrix $R\in SO(3)$ and a translation vector $T\in\mathbb{R}^3$, write down the corresponding rigid-body motion $g\in SE(3)$ and its inverse $g^{-1}$ in matrix form.
questions.answer:
$$g=\begin{pmatrix}R&T\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad g^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}R^\top&-R^\top T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Check.** $gg^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}RR^\top&-RR^\top T+T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ ✓.
**Two deductions to avoid.** Writing $R^{-1}$ instead of $R^\top$ loses half a point (they are equal, but the exam wants the orthogonality used); writing $-T$ instead of $-R^\top T$ loses a full point.
questions.extend: Read $g^{-1}$ as "undo the rotation first, then undo the (rotated) translation".

questions.q: Write down the $4\times4$ matrices $M\in SE(3)$ (for point transformation in homogeneous coordinates) for: (a) translation by $T$; (b) rotation by $R$; (c) rotation by $R$ followed by translation $T$; (d) translation by $T$ followed by rotation $R$.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $\begin{pmatrix}I&T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$
**(b)** $\begin{pmatrix}R&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$
**(c)** First rotate, then translate: $\begin{pmatrix}I&T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}R&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}R&T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ — the standard $SE(3)$ form.
**(d)** First translate, then rotate: $\begin{pmatrix}R&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I&T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}R&RT\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.extend: The order flips the translation block from $T$ to $RT$ — matrices apply **right to left**, so the first transformation is the rightmost factor.

questions.q: Define the Lie algebra of twists $\mathfrak{se}(3)$, state its dimension, and explain what the twist coordinates $\xi=(v,\omega)^\top$ mean.
questions.answer:
**Definition.** $\mathfrak{se}(3)=\left\{\hat\xi=\begin{pmatrix}\hat\omega&v\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\ \middle|\ \hat\omega\in\mathfrak{so}(3),\ v\in\mathbb{R}^3\right\}$ — the tangent space of $SE(3)$ at the identity.
**Dimension.** $\dim\mathfrak{se}(3)=3+3=6$.
**Twist coordinates.** $\xi=(v,\omega)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^6$: $\omega$ is the **angular velocity** (its direction is the rotation axis, its norm the angle) and $v$ is the **linear velocity** at the origin. Careful: $v$ is *not* the translation $T$ of the resulting motion — they are related by $T=Jv$ with $J=I+\frac{\hat\omega}{\|\omega\|^2}(1-\cos\|\omega\|)+\frac{\hat\omega^2}{\|\omega\|^3}(\|\omega\|-\sin\|\omega\|)$, and they coincide only when $\omega=0$.
**Use.** $\exp(\hat\xi)\in SE(3)$ gives an unconstrained $6$-parameter local chart, which is how poses are updated in bundle adjustment and direct SLAM.

questions.q: Let $\hat\xi=\begin{pmatrix}\hat\omega&v\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{se}(3)$ and $\theta=\|\omega\|$. Write $\exp(\hat\xi)$ in block form for (a) $\theta=0$ and (b) $\theta\neq0$. Why is the translational block generally not equal to $v$?
questions.answer:
**(a) Pure translation.** If $\omega=0$, then
$$\exp(\hat\xi)=\begin{pmatrix}I&v\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
**(b) Rotation and translation.** For $\theta\neq0$,
$$\exp(\hat\xi)=\begin{pmatrix}R&V(\omega)v\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad R=\exp(\hat\omega),$$
with
$$V(\omega)=I+\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta^2}\hat\omega+\frac{\theta-\sin\theta}{\theta^3}\hat\omega^2.$$
Equivalently, the translation is
$$T=\frac{(I-R)\hat\omega v+\omega\omega^\top v}{\|\omega\|^2}.$$
It is generally not $v$ because the body translates while its frame is continuously rotating; the instantaneous linear velocity must be integrated along that rotating frame. Only when $\omega=0$ does $V=I$ and $T=v$.
questions.extend: Do not exponentiate the rotation and copy $v$ unchanged. The coupling matrix $V(\omega)$ is the characteristic extra term of the $SE(3)$ exponential.

knowledge_points.title: Camera Motion, Concatenation and the Adjoint Map
knowledge_points.recap:
**Motion of the camera.** A moving camera is described by $g(t)=\begin{pmatrix}R(t)&T(t)\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, mapping world coordinates $X_0$ to camera coordinates $X(t)=g(t)X_0$, i.e. $X(t)=R(t)X_0+T(t)$.
**Concatenation over frames.** With $g(t_j,t_i)$ the motion from frame $i$ to frame $j$:
$$g(t_3,t_1)=g(t_3,t_2)\,g(t_2,t_1),\qquad g(t_j,t_i)^{-1}=g(t_i,t_j),$$
and the consistency rule $g(t_i,t_j)g(t_j,t_k)g(t_k,t_i)=I$ — the loop closes. Read chains right to left.
**Velocity.** Differentiating $X(t)=g(t)X_0$ and substituting $X_0=g^{-1}X$ gives $\dot X=\dot gg^{-1}X=\hat V X$, with the **twist in spatial (camera) coordinates**
$$\hat V(t)=\dot g(t)g^{-1}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\dot RR^\top&\dot T-\dot RR^\top T\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{se}(3),$$
whose upper-left block $\hat\omega=\dot RR^\top$ is the angular velocity.
**Adjoint map — transferring a twist between frames.** If two frames are related by $g$, a twist expressed in one frame becomes, in the other,
$$\hat V_2=g\,\hat V_1\,g^{-1},\qquad\text{in coordinates}\quad \xi_2=\operatorname{ad}_g(\xi_1),\ \ \operatorname{ad}_g=\begin{pmatrix}R&\hat TR\\0&R\end{pmatrix}.$$
So velocities are **not** simply rotated — the translation between the frames couples the angular part into the linear part via $\hat TR$. That coupling is the whole content of the adjoint.

questions.q: A camera observes a static scene at times $t_1,t_2,t_3$. Which relations between the rigid-body motions $g(t_j,t_i)$ are correct?
questions.answer:
**Correct.** $g(t_3,t_1)=g(t_3,t_2)g(t_2,t_1)$ — compose right to left, the earlier motion applies first. $g(t_j,t_i)^{-1}=g(t_i,t_j)$ — reversing a motion is inverting it. $g(t_1,t_2)g(t_2,t_3)g(t_3,t_1)=I$ — going round the loop returns the identity.
**Incorrect.** $g(t_3,t_1)=g(t_2,t_1)g(t_3,t_2)$ reverses the order; $SE(3)$ is not commutative, so the two products differ.

questions.q: State how the velocity of a moving camera is expressed as a twist, and how a twist is transferred between two frames (the adjoint map).
questions.answer:
**Velocity as a twist.** From $X(t)=g(t)X_0$ and $X_0=g^{-1}(t)X(t)$,
$$\dot X(t)=\dot g(t)g^{-1}(t)X(t)=\hat V(t)X(t),\qquad \hat V=\dot gg^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dot RR^\top&\dot T-\dot RR^\top T\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{se}(3).$$
The upper-left block $\hat\omega=\dot RR^\top$ is skew-symmetric — that is why the velocity lives in the Lie algebra.
**Adjoint map.** If frame 2 is related to frame 1 by $g$, then $\hat V_2=g\hat V_1g^{-1}$, which in twist coordinates reads $\xi_2=\operatorname{ad}_g(\xi_1)$ with
$$\operatorname{ad}_g=\begin{pmatrix}R&\hat TR\\0&R\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{6\times6}.$$
**Reading.** The angular part is only rotated; the linear part picks up the extra term $\hat TR\,\omega=T\times(R\omega)$, the lever-arm effect of observing the same rotation from a displaced origin.

questions.q: Two cameras have poses $(R_1,T_1)$ and $(R_2,T_2)$, each transforming a point from world coordinates into that camera's coordinates. (a) Express the rotation $R$ and translation $T$ of the relative pose that maps a point from camera-1 coordinates to camera-2 coordinates. (b) Let $C_1,C_2$ be the positions of the two cameras and $V=\overrightarrow{C_1C_2}$ the vector between them in the **world** frame; express $V$ in terms of $(R_i,T_i)$.
questions.answer:
**(a)** From $X_i=R_iX_w+T_i$ we get $X_w=R_1^\top(X_1-T_1)$, and substituting into the second camera's equation:
$$X_2=R_2R_1^\top X_1+\big(T_2-R_2R_1^\top T_1\big),$$
so
$$R=R_2R_1^\top,\qquad T=T_2-R_2R_1^\top T_1.$$
**(b)** A camera centre satisfies $0=R_iC_i+T_i$, i.e. $C_i=-R_i^\top T_i$. Hence
$$V=C_2-C_1=-R_2^\top T_2+R_1^\top T_1=R_1^\top T_1-R_2^\top T_2.$$
questions.extend: Camera **pose** $(R_i,T_i)$ and camera **centre** $C_i=-R_i^\top T_i$ are different objects — this pair of sub-questions exists precisely to test that distinction.

knowledge_points.title: Alternative Representations: Euler Angles and Quaternions
knowledge_points.recap:
**Why alternatives at all.** A rotation matrix has $9$ numbers with $6$ constraints — redundant and awkward to optimise over. The alternatives trade redundancy for singularities.
**Comparison table (worth memorising).**
$\bullet$ **Rotation matrix** — $9$ parameters, $6$ constraints ($R^\top R=I$, $\det R=1$), **no** singularities.
$\bullet$ **Axis-angle / exponential coordinates** — $3$ parameters, $0$ constraints, singular at $\theta=0$ and $\theta=2\pi$.
$\bullet$ **Euler angles** — $3$ parameters, $0$ constraints, singular at **gimbal lock**.
$\bullet$ **Unit quaternion** — $4$ parameters, $1$ constraint ($\|q\|=1$), **no** singularities.
**Euler angles.** Many conventions; the ZYX one is $R=R_z(\psi)R_y(\theta)R_x(\phi)$. **Gimbal lock:** at $\theta=\pi/2$ the matrix depends only on $(\psi-\phi)$, so one degree of freedom is lost — two of the three axes align and the parameterisation degenerates.
**Quaternions.** $q=w+xi+yj+zk$ with $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$, giving the cyclic rules $ij=k,\ jk=i,\ ki=j$ and the anti-cyclic $ji=-k,\ kj=-i,\ ik=-j$. Multiplication is **associative but not commutative**. Conjugate $q^*=w-xi-yj-zk$, norm $\|q\|=\sqrt{w^2+x^2+y^2+z^2}$, and $\|q_1q_2\|=\|q_1\|\|q_2\|$ — hence the unit quaternions form a group with $q^{-1}=q^*$.
**Rotating with quaternions.** Embed $v\in\mathbb{R}^3$ as a pure quaternion $p=v_xi+v_yj+v_zk$ and use the **sandwich product** $p\mapsto qpq^*$. Left-multiplication alone does not work: it rotates the $(w,z)$-plane too and the result stops being pure. In $qpq^*$ the $(w,z)$ rotations of $L_q$ and $R_{q^*}$ cancel while the $(x,y)$ rotations add, so the imaginary part is rotated by $2\alpha$ — which is exactly why the **half-angle** appears: $q=\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}+\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}(u_xi+u_yj+u_zk)$ for a rotation by $\theta$ about the unit axis $u$.
**Double cover.** $q$ and $-q$ give the same rotation, $(-q)p(-q)^*=qpq^*$: $S^3\to SO(3)$ is a $2{:}1$ cover.
**Why SLAM systems prefer quaternions.** Compact ($4$ vs $9$ numbers), singularity-free, trivially renormalised ($q/\|q\|$ instead of Gram–Schmidt), smooth interpolation via SLERP, and cheap composition.

questions.q: (a) For the ZYX convention, write the rotation matrix $R=R_z(\psi)R_y(\theta)R_x(\phi)$. (b) Show that for $\theta=\tfrac\pi2$ the matrix depends only on $(\psi-\phi)$ — gimbal lock. (c) Why don't quaternions suffer from gimbal lock?
questions.answer:
**(a)** With $c_\alpha=\cos\alpha$, $s_\alpha=\sin\alpha$:
$$R=\begin{pmatrix}c_\psi c_\theta&c_\psi s_\theta s_\phi-s_\psi c_\phi&c_\psi s_\theta c_\phi+s_\psi s_\phi\\s_\psi c_\theta&s_\psi s_\theta s_\phi+c_\psi c_\phi&s_\psi s_\theta c_\phi-c_\psi s_\phi\\-s_\theta&c_\theta s_\phi&c_\theta c_\phi\end{pmatrix}.$$
**(b)** At $\theta=\pi/2$, $c_\theta=0$ and $s_\theta=1$, so
$$R=\begin{pmatrix}0&c_\psi s_\phi-s_\psi c_\phi&c_\psi c_\phi+s_\psi s_\phi\\0&s_\psi s_\phi+c_\psi c_\phi&s_\psi c_\phi-c_\psi s_\phi\\-1&0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\sin(\psi-\phi)&\cos(\psi-\phi)\\0&\cos(\psi-\phi)&\sin(\psi-\phi)\\-1&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Only the difference $(\psi-\phi)$ appears: one degree of freedom is lost.
**(c)** Quaternions parameterise $SO(3)$ as $S^3/\{\pm1\}$, and the map $S^3\to SO(3)$ is smooth everywhere with no coordinate singularity. This is possible because they use $4$ parameters with $1$ constraint, avoiding the topological obstruction that forces a singularity in **any** $3$-parameter representation of $SO(3)$.
questions.extend: Gimbal lock is not a numerical accident — it is a topological necessity for every 3-parameter chart of $SO(3)$.

questions.q: Fill in the comparison table (parameters / constraints / singularities) for rotation matrix, axis-angle, Euler angles and quaternion, and briefly explain why quaternions are often preferred in SLAM systems.
questions.answer:
**Rotation matrix** — $9$ parameters, $6$ constraints ($R^\top R=I$, $\det R=1$), no singularities.
**Axis-angle** — $3$ parameters, $0$ constraints, singular at $\theta=0$ and $\theta=2\pi$.
**Euler angles** — $3$ parameters, $0$ constraints, gimbal lock.
**Quaternion** — $4$ parameters, $1$ constraint ($\|q\|=1$), no singularities.
**Why SLAM prefers quaternions.** (1) Compact — $4$ numbers instead of $9$. (2) No singularities. (3) Easy to renormalise ($q/\|q\|$) instead of re-orthogonalising with Gram–Schmidt. (4) Smooth interpolation via SLERP. (5) Cheap composition — quaternion multiplication is a handful of multiply–adds.

questions.q: Using only $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$, associativity and distributivity: (a) derive the products $ij,ji,jk,kj,ki,ik$; (b) derive the general multiplication formula $q_1q_2=w'+x'i+y'j+z'k$; (c) find $q_1,q_2$ with $q_1q_2\neq q_2q_1$.
questions.answer:
**(a)** From $ijk=-1$, right-multiplying by $k$ gives $ij(-1)=-k$, so $ij=k$. Left-multiplying $ijk=-1$ by $-i$ gives $jk=i$. From $ij=k$, left-multiplying by $-i$ gives $ik=-j$; right-multiplying by $-j$ gives $kj=-i$. From $jk=i$, left-multiplying by $-j$ gives $ji=-k$, and similarly $ki=j$.
**Summary:** cyclic $ij=k$, $jk=i$, $ki=j$; anti-cyclic $ji=-k$, $kj=-i$, $ik=-j$.
**(b)** Expanding $(w_1+x_1i+y_1j+z_1k)(w_2+x_2i+y_2j+z_2k)$:
$$w'=w_1w_2-x_1x_2-y_1y_2-z_1z_2$$
$$x'=w_1x_2+x_1w_2+y_1z_2-z_1y_2$$
$$y'=w_1y_2-x_1z_2+y_1w_2+z_1x_2$$
$$z'=w_1z_2+x_1y_2-y_1x_2+z_1w_2$$
**(c)** $q_1=i$, $q_2=j$: $q_1q_2=ij=k$ but $q_2q_1=ji=-k\neq k$.
questions.extend: The scalar part is $w_1w_2-\langle\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\rangle$ and the vector part is $w_1\mathbf{v}_2+w_2\mathbf{v}_1+\mathbf{v}_1\times\mathbf{v}_2$ — the cross product is precisely what breaks commutativity.

questions.q: (a) Verify associativity for $q_1=i,q_2=j,q_3=k$. (b) For a unit quaternion $q$, show $qq^*=1$. (c) Show $\|q_1q_2\|=\|q_1\|\|q_2\|$ and conclude that the unit quaternions form a group under multiplication.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $(ij)k=k\cdot k=k^2=-1$ and $i(jk)=i\cdot i=i^2=-1$. Equal ✓.
**(b)** $qq^*=(w+xi+yj+zk)(w-xi-yj-zk)$. Using the multiplication formula with $q_2=(w,-x,-y,-z)$: $w'=w^2+x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ and $x'=y'=z'=0$. Hence $qq^*=1$.
**(c)** $\|q_1q_2\|^2=(q_1q_2)(q_1q_2)^*=q_1q_2q_2^*q_1^*=q_1\|q_2\|^2q_1^*=\|q_2\|^2q_1q_1^*=\|q_1\|^2\|q_2\|^2$.
**Group.** Closure: $\|q_1q_2\|=1\cdot1=1$. Associativity: inherited from quaternion multiplication. Identity: $q=1$. Inverse: $q^{-1}=q^*$ since $qq^*=1$.
questions.extend: $(q_1q_2)^*=q_2^*q_1^*$ — the conjugate reverses the order, exactly like the transpose of a matrix product.

questions.q: Explain why quaternion rotation uses the sandwich product $p\mapsto qpq^*$ rather than plain left-multiplication, and why the half-angle $\alpha=\theta/2$ appears.
questions.answer:
**Why not left-multiplication.** Take $q=\cos\alpha+\sin\alpha\,k$ and the pure quaternion $p=k$ representing $e_3$. Then $L_qp=(-\sin\alpha,0,0,\cos\alpha)^\top$, whose real part $-\sin\alpha\neq0$ — the result has "leaked" out of the pure (3D) subspace, so it no longer represents a 3D vector.
**What the sandwich does.** $L_q$ rotates the $(x,y)$-plane by $+\alpha$ and the $(w,z)$-plane by $+\alpha$; right-multiplication $R_{q^*}$ rotates $(x,y)$ by $+\alpha$ and $(w,z)$ by $-\alpha$. Composing them, the $(w,z)$ rotations **cancel** (so pure quaternions stay pure) while the $(x,y)$ rotations **add** to $2\alpha$.
**Half angle.** To realise a rotation by $\theta$ we need $2\alpha=\theta$, i.e. $\alpha=\theta/2$:
$$q=\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}+\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,(u_xi+u_yj+u_zk)$$
for a rotation by $\theta$ about the unit axis $u$.
questions.extend: The doubling is also why $q$ and $-q$ give the same rotation: shifting $\theta/2$ by $\pi$ shifts $\theta$ by $2\pi$.

questions.q: (a) Show that $q$ and $-q$ give the same rotation. (b) State the $3\times3$ rotation matrix $R(q)$ for $q=(w,x,y,z)$.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $(-q)p(-q)^*=(-1)q\cdot p\cdot(-1)q^*=(-1)^2qpq^*=qpq^*$. So each rotation in $SO(3)$ corresponds to **two** unit quaternions $\pm q$ — the double cover $S^3\to SO(3)$.
**(b)** Computing $qpq^*$ for $p=i,j,k$ and reading off the columns:
$$R=\begin{pmatrix}1-2(y^2+z^2)&2(xy-wz)&2(xz+wy)\\2(xy+wz)&1-2(x^2+z^2)&2(yz-wx)\\2(xz-wy)&2(yz+wx)&1-2(x^2+y^2)\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Structure.** The diagonal is $1-2(\text{sum of the other two squares})$; the off-diagonal pairs differ only in the sign of the $w$-term, which encodes the skew (rotation-angle) part.
questions.extend: $\operatorname{trace}(R)=3-4(x^2+y^2+z^2)=4w^2-1=1+2\cos\theta$, recovering $w=\cos(\theta/2)$.

questions.q: Two orientations are represented by unit quaternions $q_0,q_1$. (a) Write the spherical linear interpolation (SLERP) $q(t)$ for $t\in[0,1]$. (b) Why must $q_1$ be replaced by $-q_1$ when $q_0^\top q_1<0$? (c) State two advantages over component-wise linear interpolation.
questions.answer:
Let $\Omega=\arccos(q_0^\top q_1)$ after choosing the signs so that $q_0^\top q_1\ge0$. Then
$$q(t)=\frac{\sin((1-t)\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}q_0+\frac{\sin(t\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}q_1.$$
If $q_0^\top q_1<0$, replacing $q_1$ by $-q_1$ does not change the represented rotation, because $q_1$ and $-q_1$ are the same element of $SO(3)$. It does select the **shorter arc** on the unit sphere $S^3$, avoiding an unnecessary long rotation.
**Advantages.** SLERP stays on $S^3$, so every intermediate quaternion has unit norm, and it moves with constant angular velocity along the shortest geodesic. Ordinary component-wise interpolation leaves the unit sphere unless it is renormalised and does not give constant angular velocity.
questions.extend: For very small $\Omega$, use normalised linear interpolation to avoid dividing by a tiny $\sin\Omega$.
